game:item-handbooktext-fruitpress: You can only use the fruit press if it is at LEAST half-full. Anything less and the press will not squish any material. Be sure to check and see if your mash can be used for anything!
item-handbooktext-acornportion: Created by portioning out a larger amount of acorns, these may be used in a wide variety of foods and meals.
item-handbooktext-agedmeat:
After being hung on a meat rack in a dry, cool environment for some time, meat slowly loses weight as its connective tissue breaks down and internal moisture evaporates. A 'crust' of fungal mold covers the exterior and must be removed before consumption.
The smaller, more tender nature of this meat makes it ill-suited for advanced meat processing techniques such as sausages.
item-handbooktext-alcoholagingguide:
All alcohols now cure over time. If it finishes curing before it begins to perish into vinegar, then it progresses to the next stage, becoming more intoxicating and filling.
Ciders and ales (usually created from curing juice or sealing it in a barrel) cure into 'strong' alcohol, then into 'fine' alcohol.
Spirits, such as brandy and whiskey (created by distilling cider/ale in a boiler), cure into 'aged' alcohol, then into 'vintage' alcohol.
'Fine' alcohol can still spoil if improperly stored - make sure it's stored someplace cool so it can 'cure' into itself instead of spoiling into vinegar. 'Vintage' alcohol lasts indefinitely, due to the concentrated alcohol content.
item-handbooktext-berrybread: A delectable treat, created by kneading 1-2 fruit and/or gelatin into a ball of dough.
item-handbooktext-birchsapportion: Collected by placing a spile into a birch log and a liquid container directly beneath it. The tree will only produce sap in April, May, and June.
item-handbooktext-breadcrumbs: Crumbled bread, the ideal breading for any fried food. When eaten in a meal, a singular handful of crumbs is as nutritious as 1/4th of a basic loaf of bread.
item-handbooktext-breadstarter:
Seal water and dried fruit in a barrel for 6 days to create yeast water, then mix it with salt and flour to create bread starter. As long as you have at least 1 L of bread starter, you can 'feed' it by kneading it with more water and flour, keeping it alive indefinitely.
Bread starter is an excellent addition to any dough.
item-handbooktext-broth:
Broth is an excellent way to stretch out many resources and make them useful for years. By simmering bones, meat, vegetables, or mushrooms in water, wonderful broths can be made. Non-bone broths must be made with partially cooked ingredients, as the roasting process is essential to imparting its flavor onto the water. Broths can be clarified by simmering them with egg white, to coagulate impurities which are then removed by skimming off the top as it cooks.
Broth is great in any dough, and it enhances most meals.
item-handbooktext-candiedfruit: Once heated enough, fruit syrup will harden and can be molded into hard candy. The fruit core provides an excellent contrast to the brittle shell. Its texture is more glassy than crystalline.
item-handbooktext-candy: Making candy is a relatively easy process. Start by kneading a sweetener, such as honey or syrup, with either peanut paste or sunflower grain... and you're done! Adding salt imparts a little extra healing, on top of the healing provided by all the sugar.
item-handbooktext-choppedmushroom: Slicing mushrooms makes them easier to put into certain foods. However, cooking them over an oven or firepit will 'cook' some of the poison out, making some mushrooms more edible.
item-handbooktext-choppedvegetable: Cutting up vegetables makes them easier to put into certain foods.
item-handbooktext-cookedchoppedmushroom: Burning a mushroom might ruin the flavor, but at least the poison cooks out. Poisonous mushrooms are best left on the firepit - non-poisonous ones are best when simmered in a saucepan or cauldron.
item-handbooktext-cookedchoppedvegetable: Cooking vegetables breaks apart their cell walls, making them far easier to digest - and usually a bit tastier, to boot. Vegetables are best when simmered in a saucepan or cauldron.
item-handbooktext-cookedmushroom: Burning a mushroom might ruin the flavor, but at least the poison cooks out. Poisonous mushrooms are best left on the firepit - non-poisonous ones are best when simmered in a saucepan or cauldron.
item-handbooktext-cookedveggie: Cooking vegetables breaks apart their cell walls, making them far easier to digest - and usually a bit tastier, to boot. Vegetables are best when simmered in a saucepan or cauldron.
item-handbooktext-dehydratedfruit: A byproduct of juicing fruit in a fruit press. Cooking these in a meal will 'rehydrate' them, providing all the nutrition of raw fruit.
item-handbooktext-dough: Flour can be mixed with water from a liquid container like usual, but kneading allows more ingredients to be combined together. In addition to water, milk, lard, and broth may be used to create dough. Optionally, lard/cooking oil and yeast starter can be added in. Adding any liquids beyond water will add small amounts of nutrition and healing to the finished bread product (including pies).
item-handbooktext-dressing:
An emulsified mixture of oil and vinegar creates a basic salad dressing mixture. When kneading the dressing, different variants can be made with different ingredients.
Kneading egg white further stabilizes it and adds volume, creating smooth salad dressing.
Adding a sweetener such as honey or syrup can give the dressing a rich, deep flavor, resulting in sweet salad dressing.
For an umami flavor, add fish or soy sauce to create savory salad dressing.
Combining all possible dressing ingredients will make the deluxe salad dressing, with the most complex flavor profile.
item-handbooktext-driedseaweed: A critical ingredient in sushi, seaweed sheets are produced in a manner similar to paper. Ground to a paste, then washed with water, formed into sheets, and air-dried, the resulting sheets are roasted in an oven to maximize flavor and longevity.
item-handbooktext-dryfruit: The simplest way to preserve fruit long-term. Cooking these in a meal will 'rehydrate' them, providing all the nutrition of raw fruit.
item-handbooktext-dumpling: A widespread food where cooked dough is wrapped around a filling. Nearly any chopped food item can be kneaded with soft dough to make dumplings. They can be baked on their own, but are best when added to meals - especially soup. Unlike other expanded foods, up to 3 soup meal slots can be used for dumplings.
item-handbooktext-fermentedfish: The fish meat has begun fermenting and reeks with a sharp, fishy odor. Somehow, it looks like there are bits of bone in this... slop pile. Juice it quickly, before the crows come.
item-handbooktext-fishnugget: Fish, like any meat, can be tenderized via direct blunt force. Doing so makes it tastier and easier to digest. Chopped fish nuggets can be used in more foods and meals than smashed fish fillets.
item-handbooktext-fishsauce: An ancient condiment made from salted, fermented fish. Fish sauce that has been briefly fermented has a strong fishy flavor, which turns nutty and savory with extended fermentation.
item-handbooktext-foodoilportion:
Cooking oils are a versatile kind of liquid fat, used primarily in cooking. However, its lubricating qualities allow oil a secondary use for reducing friction in machinery.

Certain materials are easier to juice than others.
Flax grain, rice grain, sunflower grain and seeds require the most material (128 per 10 L).
Legumes such as peanuts and soybeans require less (64 per 10 L).
Olives require the fewest materials, as they are quite juicy (32 per 10 L).
item-handbooktext-fruitbar: A high energy food, compact and easily transportable. It is made by kneading a stabilizing agent, such as grain or nuts, with fruit, filling (such as gelatin or yogurt), and sweetener (such as honey or syrup).
item-handbooktext-fruitsyrupportion: By boiling fruit juice, the sugar to water ratio increases as water evaporates. This sweet condiment can be used as a topping for many foods and meals, or as a bonding agent for breading food.
item-handbooktext-fryingguide: Almost anything can be fried, if you put your mind to it. Get started by taking a basic ingredient, such as cheese, vegetables, meat, or boiled eggs, then knead it with a bonding agent such as food oil, honey, lard, liquid egg, or syrup, some flour to form a mild crust, and a handful of bread crumbs to finalize the breading. This breaded item can be further kneaded with lard or oil to enhance its flavor, then baked in an oven- but it may burn if left unattended. Simmering it with lard or oil will result in a perfectly fried food every time, and cauldrons make it easy to fry in bulk.
item-handbooktext-gelatin: First, simmer bones in water to start releasing the collagens and make bone broth. Take that bone broth and simmer it with more bones to start gelatinizing it and reducing its proteins into peptides, creating pre-gelatin. Finally, simmer pre-gelatin with more bones to create raw gelatin, a flavorless hydrogel. At this point, it can be simmered with any juice or syrup to make flavored gelatin.
item-handbooktext-gozinaki: A simple, brittle confection made by kneading nuts or sunflower grain with honey, then baked until hard. It can then be further sweetened with a variety of toppings, such as peanut butter/sauce, syrup, or additional honey.
item-handbooktext-hardlard: Now free from its confines, these bricks of lard may be easily stored, transported, and used later.
item-handbooktext-hardlardliquid: Liquid lard that has hardened, but is still inside of a liquid container. While holding the container, press Ctrl+ to empty it onto the ground, producing a hardened lard brick.
item-handbooktext-hardtack: A dense, long-lasting cracker made by kneading water or broth with flour and salt. Egg liquid may be optionally added for additional flavor, but don't expect anything tasty. These crackers are baked for extended periods under high heat, hardening them and making them nearly intolerable to consume. They can cheaply fill out a meal, so they are carried for long voyages.
item-handbooktext-juiceprocessingguide:
Fruit juice is a base liquid with many resulting outputs.
If allowed to spoil, it ferments into vinegar and acidifies.
When sealed into a barrel or bottle, juice cures over time into 'cider' (the exact name varies based on the fruit used).
Lastly, juice may be simmered in a saucepan or cauldron to concentrate it into fruit syrup.
item-handbooktext-lard:
Liquid animal fat, rendered by boiling chunks of fat in water. Its property of producing very little smoke when cooked and its flavor makes it ideal for frying foods. The fatty content makes dough more flaky, too.
Note: Cooking 1 chunk of fat results in 0.2L of lard, and most recipes in Expanded Foods only require 0.1L of lard - this effectively doubles how much fat you can use in recipes.
item-handbooktext-limeegg: Water-glassing preserves fresh eggs by submerging them in lime, which seals the eggshell and maintains its texture. Eggs can be water-glassed nearly indefinitely, but the lime must be regularly refreshed.
item-handbooktext-maplesapportion: Collected by placing a spile into a maple log and a liquid container directly beneath it. The tree will only produce sap in January, Feburary, and March.
item-handbooktext-meatnugget: Meat can be tenderized via direct blunt force. Doing so makes it tastier and easier to digest. Chopped meat nuggets can be used in more foods and meals than tenderized meat.
item-handbooktext-muffin: A moist cupcake with a variety of flavors. By kneading soft dough with fruit, pumpkin, carrots, and/or gelatin, then baking the resulting batter, the muffin develops a browned crust that slightly caramelizes any exposed ingredients. It can then be topped with sweetener, such as honey, syrup, peanut sauce, or peanut butter.
item-handbooktext-pasta:
An unleavened dough, cut into noodle form, then cooked and prepared with just about any ingredient. Fresh pasta is made by kneading flour and liquid egg, then flattening it into a sheet using an instrument. This dough sheet is then cut into noodles, which can be cooked over a firepit to make soup or hot pasta. Alternately, the noodles may be simmered with water to cook them, after which they may be mixed with other ingredients, or added to stew.
Cut noodles can also be baked in an oven to dry them out into a more shelf-stable form, that can later be used anywhere the normal cut noodles can be.
item-handbooktext-pasteurizedmilkportion: Heating milk to slightly less than 100 °C will destroy the microorganisms within, reducing risk of disease and extending shelf life. The lack of bacteria makes it optimal for kneading with yogurt starter, so the yogurt's bacteria can ferment properly.
item-handbooktext-peanut: By roasting peanuts in an oven, their nutty flavor is enhanced and the skins become easier to remove. The roasted kernels are delicious and can be ground into very useful peanut paste, while the leftover skins can be used as animal feed or fertilizer.
item-handbooktext-peanutliquid-butter: Made by kneading peanut paste and cooking oil, the emulsified result is spreadable and high in calories. It can be sweetened further with honey or syrup, and salt makes all of the butter's flavors more pronounced.
item-handbooktext-peanutliquid-paste: Due to its high oil content, grinding peanuts results in a crunchy paste. This is edible enough on its own, but is a fantastic base for making peanut butter or peanut sauce.
item-handbooktext-peanutliquid-sauce: A specialized sauce used mainly for dipping or topping food. Created by kneading peanut paste with a savory sauce such as fish or soy sauce, a sweetener such as honey or syrup, and water. The result is a thick sauce with balanced flavors.
item-handbooktext-pemmican: An unappetizing, but palatable mixture of fat, meat, and fruit that lasts an extremely long time. Made by kneading fat or lard with fruit and meat nuggets. Unlike other foods, the sheer quantity of pemmican being created results in 2 chunks being output instead of 1. Mashed pemmican may be heated into a brick form and stored or eaten on its own, or it may be added to stews. Cooked pemmican may not be added to meals, as it is already cooked.
item-handbooktext-plaindoughball: Similar to regular dough, but the addition of liquid egg has greatly changed the texture and composition. In addition to kneading a liquid (such as broth, lard, milk, or water) with flour and liquid egg, adding bread starter and oil/lard results in a truly delectable bread treat. A fantastic base for making other foods.
item-handbooktext-sausage:
A ground meat product that is preserved with fat. Basic sausage is made by kneading meat nuggets with fat or lard, but cheese makes an excellent filling. Adding salt during the kneading process will make curable sausage, which can be cured to last an extremely long time.
Raw (ie. non-curing) sausage may be hung from a meat rack in a manner similar to aged meat in order to 'dry age' it. The aging process vastly improves its flavor and texture.
item-handbooktext-soulstormbrew:
The highly addictive product of Projekt SoulStorm™.
Created by kneading a host of healthy, nutritious ingredients together to form the illustrious SoulStorm Slop™, an energy-rich solution that needs to be simmered with noble, ancestral, and proprietary ingredients to make Refined SoulStorm Slop™. At this point, the Slop™ can be distilled into pure, delicious, energizing SoulStorm Brew™!!!
item-handbooktext-soulstormbrew2: 'THE TASTIEST ENERGY DRINK ON THE PLANET!!! DRINK, DRINK, DRINK!!!'
item-handbooktext-soymilk: Place the soaked soybeans in your crafting grid to de-shell them, then combine with 1 L of water in the crafting grid to wet them. Grind the wettened soybeans in a quern to blend them, then juice the mixture in a fruit press to make soy milk.
item-handbooktext-soyprep:
Creating soy sauce or soy milk is a multi-step process. First, soak soybeans in water for 3 days. The next steps depend on the desired result.

Making Soy Sauce
Roast the soaked soybeans in an oven, then grind the roasted soybeans in a quern. Mix the soybean powder with any grain to culture it. Soak the cultured soybeans with brine for 1 week to make a soybean slurry, which can be juiced in a fruit press into soy sauce.

Making Soy Milk
Place the soaked soybeans in your crafting grid to de-shell them, then combine with 1 L of water in the crafting grid to wet them. Grind the wettened soybeans in a quern to blend them, then juice the mixture in a fruit press to make soy milk.
item-handbooktext-soysauce: Roast the soaked soybeans in an oven, then grind the roasted soybeans in a quern. Mix the soybean powder with any grain to culture it. Soak the cultured soybeans with brine for 1 week to make a soybean slurry, which can be juiced in a fruit press into soy sauce.
item-handbooktext-stuffedpepper:
These giant peppers are well-suited for additional filling. In addition to bell pepper, take a basic ingredient, such as cheese, dried fruit, meat or vegetables, then knead it and bake the result.
Bell peppers may also be breaded. In addition to the bell pepper and basic ingredient, knead in a bonding agent such as food oil, honey, lard, liquid egg, or syrup, some flour to form a mild crust, and a handful of bread crumbs to finalize the breading. Breaded stuffed bell pepper can be further kneaded with lard or oil to enhance its flavor, then baked in an oven- but it may burn if left unattended. Simmering it with lard or oil will result in a perfectly fried food every time, and cauldrons make it easy to fry in bulk.
item-handbooktext-sushi: A specialized food ideal for coastal societies. Rice and edible seaweed sheets are kneaded, with chopped vegetables and fish optionally added. Once rolled, additional toppings such as honey, tree syrup, or sauces may be drizzled for more flavor.
item-handbooktext-trailmix:
A nutritious, long-lasting, easily stored snack mix. It provides almost every nutrition type, making it excellent for keeping your maximum HP up on a long journey.
Trail mix comes in four major varieties: Cheesy, fruity, meaty (or beany, for vegetarians), and nutty. Knead cheese, cured meat nuggets (or soybeans, for vegetarians), dried fruit, and nuts. The kind of trail mix that is made depends on the ingredient that makes up the majority of the recipe.
item-handbooktext-treesyrupportion: By boiling tree sap, the sugar to water ratio increases as water evaporates. This sweet condiment can be used as a topping for many foods and meals, or as a bonding agent for breading food.
item-handbooktext-vegetablejuiceportion: Made by juicing a variety of vegetables, this liquid can be used to make a variety of vegetable-flavored gelatins, or as stock in pilaf, hot pasta, or soup.
item-handbooktext-yogurt:
Cultivating bacteria by fermenting curdled milk with fruit creates yogurt starter, a highly active bacterial base. Simmering the yogurt starter with pasteurized milk over a low heat will inoculate the bacteria, kickstarting the fermentation process and creating fermenting yogurt. Once this yogurt is allowed to ferment in a sealed barrel or a bottle until you have the final plain yogurt product. At this point, plain yogurt may be kneaded with any kind of sweetener to make flavored yogurt.
Plain or flavored yogurt can last almost indefinitely if stored properly - it will cure into yogurt starter instead of rot, and this yogurt starter can be used to repeatedly restart the above process.
itemdesc-dressing-basic: Zesty and oily, this simple dressing enhances any salad or pasta.
itemdesc-dressing-deluxe: Rich and deep with a velvety texture, fit for a king. The key to making the ultimate salad or pasta.
itemdesc-dressing-savory: Rich and tangy, the depth of flavor is intense. Ideal on salad or pasta.
itemdesc-dressing-sweet: Thin and sweet, also known as a vinaigrette. This stuff makes salads and pasta really pop!
itemdesc-driedseaweed-washed: Use your hands to shape into sheets.
itemdesc-hardlardliquid: Dump out a bucket full of hardened lard to acquire a brick of lard.
